fetched_contents.text: Molecular Mechanisms of Ultraviolet Radiation-Induced DNA Damage and Repair Abstract DNA is one of the prime molecules, and its stability is of utmost importance for proper functioning and existence of all living systems. Genotoxic chemicals and radiations exert adverse effects on genome stability. Ultraviolet radiation (UVR) (mainly UV-B: 280–315 nm) is one of the powerful agents that can alter the normal state of life by inducing a variety of mutagenic and cytotoxic DNA lesions such as cyclobutane-pyrimidine dimers (CPDs), 6-4 photoproducts (6-4PPs), and their Dewar valence isomers as well as DNA strand breaks by interfering the genome integrity. To counteract these lesions, organisms have developed a number of highly conserved repair mechanisms such as photoreactivation, base excision repair (BER), nucleotide excision repair (NER), and mismatch repair (MMR). Additionally, double-strand break repair (by homologous recombination and nonhomologous end joining), SOS response, cell-cycle checkpoints, and programmed cell death (apoptosis) are also operative in various organisms with the expense of specific gene products. This review deals with UV-induced alterations in DNA and its maintenance by various repair mechanisms. 1. Introduction The stratospheric ozone layer is continuously depleting due to the release of atmospheric pollutants such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), chlorocarbons (CCs), and organo-bromides (OBs). Consequently there is an increase in the incidence of UV radiation (UVR) on the Earth's surface [1] which is one of the most effective and carcinogenic exogenous agents that can interact with DNA and alter the genome integrity and may affect the normal life processes of all organisms ranging from prokaryotes to mammals [2–10]. However, wide variations in tolerance to UV-B among species and taxonomic groups have been reported. Moreover, ozone depletion followed by increased UV exposure has been predicted to continue throughout most of this century [11]. In all the groups of UVR (i.e., UV-A: 315–400 nm; UV-B: 280–315 nm; UV-C: <280 nm) UV-B radiation produces adverse effects on diverse habitats, even though most of the extraterrestrial UV-B is absorbed by the stratospheric ozone [12]. UV-A radiation has a poor efficiency in inducing DNA damage, because it is not absorbed by native DNA. UV-A and visible light energy (up to 670–700 nm) are able to generate singlet oxygen (1O2) that can damage DNA via indirect photosensitizing reactions [13]. UV-C radiation is quantitatively absorbed by oxygen and ozone in the Earth's atmosphere, hence does not show much harmful effects on biota. Solar UV radiation is responsible for a wide range of biological effects including alteration in the structure of protein, DNA, and many other biologically important molecules, chronic depression of key physiological processes, and acute physiological stress leading to either reduction in growth and cell division, pigment bleaching, N2 fixation, energy production, or photoinhibition of photosynthesis in several organisms [3, 9, 10]. It has been documented that UV-B severely affects survival, fecundity, and sex-ratio in several intertidal copepods [14]. One of the most prominent targets of solar UV-radiation is cellular DNA, which absorbs UV-B radiation and causes adverse effects on living systems such as bacteria [15, 16], cyanobacteria [17], phytoplankton [18], macroalgae [19], plants [20], animals, and humans [21–23]. Although UV-B radiation has less than 1% of total solar energy, it is a highly active component of the solar radiation that brings about chemical modification in DNA and changes its molecular structure by the formation of dimers. Certain UV-absorbing pigments are produced by a number of organisms as a first line of defense; however, they are unable to avoid UV-radiation completely from reaching DNA in superficial tissue [28–32]. Certain enzymes, such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), peroxidase (POD), and scavengers such as vitamin C, B, and E, cysteine, and glutathione play an additional role in defense against UV radiation [33]. However, as a second line of defense several organisms have developed a number of specific and highly conserved repair mechanisms such as photoreactivation, excision repair, mismatch repair (MMR), double strand break (DSB) repair and certain other mechanisms like damage tolerance (dimer bypass), SOS (save our soul) response, checkpoint activation, and programmed cell death (PCD) or apoptosis (Figure 1) that efficiently remove DNA lesions ensuring the genomic integrity [22]. Plants are unique in the obligatory nature of their exposure to UVR; it is also conceivable that they may also have evolved certain efficient repair mechanisms for the elimination of UV-induced DNA damage. However, a number of questions concerning the basic phenomena of the DNA repair in plants remain to be elucidated. In the following, we discuss the molecular mechanisms of UV-induced DNA damage and repair mechanism (s) operative in various organisms. 2. UV-Induced DNA Damage Induction of DNA damage by solar UVR is a key event that drastically influences the normal life processes of all organisms. A number of endogenous factors such as free radicals [34] generated during metabolic processes as well as exogenous factors such as UV or ionizing radiations [35] are known to interfere with genome integrity. DNA damage results in (i) misincorporation of bases during replication process, (ii) hydrolytic damage, which results in deamination of bases, depurination, and depyrimidination [36], (iii) oxidative damage, caused by direct interaction of ionizing radiations (IR) with the DNA molecules, as well as mediated by UV radiation-induced free radicals or reactive oxygen species [37, 38], and (iv) alkylating agents that may result in modified bases [36, 39]. fetched_contents.text: Microbial Dose-Response Curves and Disinfection Efficacy Models Revisited Abstract The same term “dose-response curve” describes the relationship between the number of ingested microbes or their logarithm, and the probability of acute illness or death (type I), and between a disinfectant’s dose and the targeted microbe’s survival ratio (type II), akin to survival curves in thermal and non-thermal inactivation kinetics. The most common model of type I curves is the cumulative form of the beta-Poisson distribution which is sometimes indistinguishable from the lognormal or Weibull distribution. The most notable survival kinetics models in static disinfection are of the Chick-Watson-Hom’s kind. Their published dynamic versions, however, should be viewed with caution. A microbe population’s type II dose-response curve, static and dynamic, can be viewed as expressing an underlying spectrum of individual vulnerabilities (or resistances) to the particular disinfectant. Therefore, such a curve can be described mathematically by the flexible Weibull distribution, whose scale parameter is a function of the disinfectant’s intensity, temperature, and other factors. But where the survival ratio’s drop is so steep that the static dose-response curve resembles a step function, the Fermi distribution function becomes a suitable substitute. The utility of the CT (or Ct) concept primarily used in water disinfection is challenged on theoretical grounds and its limitations highlighted. It is suggested that stochastic models of microbial inactivation could be used to link the fates of individual viruses or bacteria to their manifestation in the survival curve’s shape. Although the emphasis is on viruses and bacteria, most of the discussion is relevant to fungi, protozoa, and perhaps worms too. Keywords: Kinetics, Viruses, Bacteria, CT (or Ct), Chick-Watson-Hom’s models, Distribution functions, Stochastic models, Survival models Introduction COVID 19 [43, 45] transmission through consumption of contaminated food has not been an issue in the current crisis, but other kinds of viruses remain a health hazard [3, 10, 52]. Conventional food preservation methods, primarily targeting cellular organisms especially bacteria, have been apparently efficient in destroying viruses as well [4]. However, meat-processing plants have recently emerged as hotspots in the pandemic spread in rural areas, and food service operations been identified as potential culprits of its spread among humans. Thus, not surprisingly, disinfection of personnel, produce, clothing, air, tools, equipment, or any surface that humans can be in contact with has recently become a common practice and increasingly mandated by health authorities. There is a very rich body of scientific and technical literature on disinfection. Being an integral part of medicine, water, and air purification, and an important aspect of the food, pharmaceutical, and other industries, the various aspects of disinfection, including its kinetics, have been extensively investigated at every relevant level form the molecular to the epidemiological. The objective of this review is neither to evaluate and compare the efficacy of the various available disinfection methods and explain their underlying biological/chemical/biochemical/physical principles, nor to discuss the engineering aspects of their implementation. This work has the very limited scope to highlight and assess the theoretical implications of the similarities and dissimilarities between kinetic models of water, air and surface disinfection, and those used to quantify the efficacy of food preservation methods, thermal and non-thermal. Although special attention will be given to viruses and bacteria, we should always keep in mind that most of the technologies and agents used for their disinfection are also effective against other biological contaminants. Terms and Definitions Disinfection, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), is a “process that eliminates many or all pathogenic microorganisms, except bacterial spores, on inanimate objects.” It differs from sterilization, which “eliminates all forms of microbial life” and from cleaning (also called sanitation) which is “the removal of visible soil (e.g., organic and inorganic material) from objects and surfaces and normally is accomplished manually or mechanically using water with detergents or enzymatic products.” Disinfectants, according to Wikipedia, are “chemical agents designed to inactivate or destroy microorganisms on inert surfaces,” which may include fresh produce [26]. But the term also applies to chemical agents used to disinfect water and air [1, 17, 21, 43, 44, 46, 49], ultraviolet (UV) light [23], other forms of radiation [14, 15], and even cold plasma [31]. Dose in our context can be defined as the quantity of disinfectant used in a particular application. Originally, it referred to an amount of medicine prescribed to (dosis in Greek) or of ingested poison by a human. Now, the term is also used for the amount of disinfectant administered to a targeted microorganism or the medium in which it may reside or the surface on which it may be present (see below). Dose-response curve (or exposure-response relationship) according to Wikipedia “describes the magnitude of the response of an organism, as a function of exposure to a stimulus or stressor after a certain exposure time.” The response is commonly expressed as the percent of inactivated organisms and hence has the range of 0 to 100% (see below). It is used to compare disinfectants’ potency; the lower the LD50 the higher is the agent toxicity or treatment efficacy. fetched_contents.text: Pulsed and continuous light UV LED: microbial inactivation, electrical, and time efficiency Introduction The recent emergence of deep UV light emitting diodes (LEDs) has increased the potential application of UV inactivation by offering tailored wavelengths and wavelength combinations, low power requirements, flexible design configurations, pulsing, and improved robustness over UV LP lamps without the mercury (Song et al., 2016; Malley, 2004; Beck et al., 2017; Aoyagi et al., 2011; Oguma et al., 2013; Bowker et al., 2011; Rattanakul and Oguma, 2018; Malayeri et al., 2016). UV is particularly effective against chlorine-resistant pathogens including bacterial biofilm species such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and protozoan parasites such as Cryptosporidium (Clancy et al., 2004; Malayeri et al., 2016). Because microorganisms are differentially susceptible to disinfectants and there are myriad applications of disinfection (i.e., point of entry public water systems, hospital water tanks, industrial applications, residential point of use, etc.), demand for new technologies and approaches for targeting specific microorganisms is high (Hijnen et al., 2006). A growing number of studies have explored the application of UV LEDs in drinking water disinfection. Comparing UV LEDs to LP lamps can be done two different ways: (1) on a fluence-basis and (2) on an electrical basis. A comparison on a fluence basis simply allows for the direct comparison of a microorganism's response to various applied fluences without incorporating any energy use into the comparison. However, an electrical-basis comparison incorporates the amount of energy required for one order of magnitude response decrease in concentration in the log-linear response region of a log reduction curve. In general, even if UV LEDs are more efficacious than LP lamps on a fluence-basis, UV LEDs will require improvements in their efficiencies to near 25–39% in order to achieve similar performance to UV LP lamps on an electrical basis (Beck et al., 2017). While one UV LED manufacturer has produced a 280 nm UV LED with a reported external quantum efficiency (EQE) of approximately 20% and three manufacturers have achieved 10–12% EQE (at approximately 280 nm), current efficiencies typically range from 0.01 to 7% EQE between 220 and 285 nm (Kneissl et al., 2019). The EQE is simply a ratio of the number of electrons applied to the UV LED and the number of photons escaping. This does not take into account the electrical efficiency of a device or any thermal management systems; it is simply a tool used to discuss the efficiency of a UV LED chip. Germicidal effectiveness on a fluence-basis favors wavelengths which correspond closely to the peak absorbance of both nucleic acids and cellular proteins (near 260–280 nm and below 230 nm, respectively); however, effectiveness on an electrical-basis favors higher intensity output UV LEDs (Würtele et al., 2011; Aoyagi et al., 2011; Oguma et al., 2013; Chatterley and Linden, 2009). On a fluence-basis, studies have shown that nominal 255–285 nm UV-LEDs induce inactivation rate constants for E. coli ranging from 0.15 to 0.81 cm2/mJ (Chatterley and Linden, 2010; Bowker et al., 2011; Malayeri et al., 2016; Oguma et al., 2016; Oguma et al., 2013; Rattanakul and Oguma, 2018; Nyangaresi et al., 2018) with the highest values corresponding to wavelengths closest to the peak of the E. coli action spectrum (266 nm) (Beck et al., 2016). The unique response of each microorganism to various UV wavelengths is due to each microbe's distinctive composition of proteins and nucleic acids; this concept is referred to as the action spectrum of a microorganism (Sinsheimer, 1954; Sinha and Häder, 2002; Minton and Friedberg, 1974; Smith, 1962). Across this wavelength range, the rate constants are comparable to those induced by UV LP lamps at 254 nm (0.20–0.81 cm2/mJ) (Malayeri et al., 2016; Rattanakul and Oguma, 2018). P. aeruginosa inactivation by 265–285 nm UV LEDs induce inactivation rate constants ranging from 0.51 to 0.74 cm2/mJ (Rattanakul and Oguma, 2018). The wavelength range explored in previous studies does not correspond to the peak action spectrum sensitivity for P. aeruginosa which peaks near 258 nm (Lakretz et al., 2010). Similar to E. coli, P. aeruginosa UV LED rate constants are comparable to those induced by UV LP lamps (0.45–0.77 cm2/mJ) (Rattanakul and Oguma, 2018; Malayeri et al., 2016). MS-2 inactivation by 255–285 nm UV LEDs induce inactivation rate constants ranging from 0.029 to 0.076 cm2/mJ (Bowker et al., 2011; Aoyagi et al., 2011; Sholtes et al., 2016; Jenny et al., 2014; Simons et al., 2014; Oguma et al., 2016) with higher rate constants nearer 262 nm. This trend corresponds to the peak action spectrum sensitivity for MS-2 (Beck et al., 2015). The lowest inactivation rate constants for all microorganisms occurred at the tail end of the germicidal spectrum, near 285 nm. Because different wavelengths can target differing critical cellular components (i.e., proteins vs nucleic acids) (Malley, 2004; Rattanakul and Oguma, 2018; Malayeri et al., 2016; Falkinham et al., 2015; Hijnen et al., 2006), applying various UV wavelengths is considered a more effective strategy than applying UV light at only one wavelength (Hijnen et al., 2006; Linden et al., 2007). Main mechanisms through which pulsed UV radiation inactivates microorganisms

Pulsed UV radiation inactivates microorganisms primarily through direct DNA damage, reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and indirect damage pathways, while microbial repair and resistance mechanisms can reduce the effectiveness of these processes. The evidence also shows that pulse characteristics such as duty cycle and pulse duration can influence how UV photons are delivered and how damage accumulates over time.

First, the primary direct DNA damage pathway induced by UV photons is the formation of helix-distorting lesions in DNA. The review evidence states that UV-induced DNA damage occurs most notably through the induction of cyclobutane-pyrimidine dimers (CPDs), 6-4 photoproducts (6-4PPs), and their Dewar valence isomers, as well as DNA strand breaks [N1-F1]. This damage disrupts DNA structure and function, making it a central target of UV inactivation. The same source also notes that DNA is one of the prime molecules affected by UV radiation and that organisms use repair mechanisms such as photoreactivation, base excision repair (BER), nucleotide excision repair (NER), mismatch repair (MMR), and double-strand break repair to counteract these lesions [N1-F1]. This implies that direct DNA damage is a core mechanism, but it is not the only one.

Second, UV radiation can also generate reactive oxygen species and indirect damage pathways. The evidence explicitly states that oxidative damage can be caused by direct interaction of ionizing radiations with DNA molecules, as well as mediated by UV radiation-induced free radicals or reactive oxygen species [N1-F1]. It also reports that irradiation with 254-nm UVC has been associated with ROS generation involved in the germicidal mechanism [N1-R3]. This means that even when UV photons do not directly hit DNA, they can still damage microorganisms by creating ROS that oxidize DNA or other cellular components. However, the evidence provided does not give a detailed mechanism of ROS-mediated inactivation beyond the general statement that ROS are involved, so this point should be treated as established but not fully elaborated in the available material.

Third, microbial repair and resistance mechanisms can mitigate inactivation. The evidence clearly identifies photoreactivation and dark repair as mechanisms that reverse UV-induced DNA damage, and it notes that some microorganisms require visible light for photoreactivation while others can repair DNA without light [N4-R4]. The review also lists several repair pathways, including BER, NER, MMR, double-strand break repair, the SOS response, cell-cycle checkpoints, and programmed cell death [N1-F1]. These mechanisms reduce the net effect of UV exposure because they can repair or tolerate some damage. In addition, the evidence mentions scavengers such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), peroxidase (POD), and antioxidants like vitamin C, B, and E, cysteine, and glutathione, which help defend against UV radiation [N1-F1]. These defense systems further reduce UV inactivation efficacy by limiting oxidative stress and damage accumulation.

Fourth, pulse characteristics influence photon delivery and damage accumulation. The pulsed-UV literature indicates that pulsed UV LEDs are being studied for microbial inactivation, and one review states that pulsed UV light is pulsed several times per second with pulse durations between 100 ns and 2 ms [N3-R5]. A key result is that 255–285 nm UV LEDs can inactivate microorganisms in drinking water, and the evidence notes that the wavelength range explored corresponds to the peak absorbance of nucleic acids and cellular proteins [N3-F3]. However, the evidence also suggests that the relationship between pulsed delivery and inactivation is not yet fully resolved: one study found no difference in disinfection between pulsed and continuous UV LEDs, while another reported that pulsed UV-C radiation at 260 nm produced significantly greater log reductions than continuous UV-C for E. coli and B. subtilis [N3-R1][N3-R2]. This implies that pulse characteristics may affect inactivation depending on the microorganism, wavelength, and duty cycle, but the available evidence is mixed and still being investigated.

In summary, the main mechanisms are: direct DNA damage via CPDs, 6-4PPs, and strand breaks [N1-F1]; ROS-mediated indirect damage [N1-F1][N1-R3]; repair by photoreactivation, dark repair, BER, NER, MMR, and other pathways [N1-F1][N4-R4]; and the influence of pulse duration, duty cycle, and wavelength on photon delivery and damage accumulation [N3-R5][N3-F3]. The evidence supports a composite picture in which UV inactivation depends on both direct and indirect damage, while repair and resistance reduce the overall effectiveness.

How irradiation intensity affects inactivation processes and outcomes

Irradiation intensity affects inactivation processes and outcomes through its relationship with irradiance, dose, and microbial survival; through kinetic models that shape the dose-response curve; through thresholds separating inactivation from sublethal exposure; and through interactions with microbial physiology and repair mechanisms.

First, irradiance, dose, and microbial survival are closely related. The dose-response concept is described as the relationship between the number of microbes or their logarithm and the probability of inactivation, with the same term used for both acute illness/death and microbial survival after disinfectant exposure [N2-F2]. The evidence also states that survival curves show the relationship between UV-C treatment and microbial survivors at specific fluence levels, and that inactivation kinetics can be modeled to estimate survivors after treatment [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This means that higher irradiance can increase the dose delivered more quickly, but the actual survival outcome depends on the total UV dose and how the microorganism responds to that dose. The evidence also notes that the survival curve can resemble a step function when the drop is steep, in which case the Fermi distribution becomes suitable [N2-F2], while flexible Weibull and stochastic models can describe the underlying vulnerability spectrum [N2-F2]. These findings show that intensity is not the only determinant: dose accumulation and microbial response matter as much as the instantaneous irradiance.

Second, kinetic models change the dose-response curve. The evidence explicitly states that the most notable survival kinetics models in static disinfection are of the Chick-Watson-Hom kind, and that their dynamic versions should be viewed with caution [N2-F2]. It also notes that the flexible Weibull distribution is a useful mathematical description of the survival curve, with the scale parameter depending on disinfectant intensity, temperature, and other factors [N2-F2]. This implies that intensity can shift the shape of the curve: higher intensity may reduce the number of surviving organisms more rapidly, but the exact relationship depends on the model and the microbial population. The evidence also mentions stochastic models that link individual microbial fates to the survival curve’s shape [N2-F2], which suggests that intensity can influence not only the overall survival fraction but also the variability in inactivation outcomes across individuals.

Third, there are clear thresholds for inactivation versus sublethal exposure. The evidence states that the same dose-response curve describes both type I (illness/death) and type II (microbial survival) relationships, and that the response is commonly expressed as the percent of inactivated organisms [N2-F2]. The term “LD50” is used as a median lethal dose, where lower LD50 means higher efficacy [N2-F2]. In practice, the evidence reports that UV-C can reduce bacterial populations by several log10 units at high fluence levels, such as 7 log10 reduction at 56 J/mL for Listeria monocytogenes [N2-R3]. This shows that intensity determines whether the exposure is sublethal or lethal: low-intensity exposure may leave many microbes viable, while higher-intensity exposure can push the system into a steep inactivation phase. The evidence also supports the idea that intensity can shift the response from a gradual decrease in survivors to a more abrupt drop [N2-F2].

Fourth, intensity interacts with microbial physiology and repair. The evidence shows that microorganisms have repair mechanisms such as photoreactivation and dark repair that can reduce the net inactivation effect [N4-R4][N4-R1]. It also notes that organisms use BER, NER, MMR, double-strand break repair, the SOS response, checkpoints, and programmed cell death to counteract UV damage [N1-F1]. This means that higher intensity can overwhelm repair capacity, but if repair mechanisms are effective, they can offset some of the damage. The evidence further indicates that microbial tolerance to UV-B varies across species and taxonomic groups, and that increased UV exposure can be predicted to continue throughout much of this century because of ozone depletion [N1-F1]. This physiological variability implies that intensity does not act uniformly: some microbes may survive higher doses because they repair faster or have more resistance, while others may be killed more readily.

In conclusion, irradiation intensity affects inactivation by changing the dose delivered, altering the shape of the dose-response curve, crossing inactivation thresholds, and interacting with microbial repair and physiology. The evidence supports the use of kinetic models, the importance of intensity-dependent scale parameters, and the distinction between sublethal and lethal exposure [N2-F2]. It also shows that microbial repair mechanisms can reduce the effectiveness of UV treatment even when intensity is high [N4-R4][N1-F1].

Practical implications of intensity and protocol design for microbial control

The practical implications of intensity and protocol design for microbial control include choosing optimal intensity ranges for different microorganisms and environments, balancing intensity, dose, and system throughput, accounting for operational factors such as suspension state and turbidity, and meeting disinfection standards and validation requirements.

First, optimal intensity ranges vary with microorganisms and environments. The evidence shows that different wavelengths and intensities are more effective for different microorganisms because each has a distinctive composition of proteins and nucleic acids, leading to different action spectra [N3-F3]. It also reports that 255–285 nm UV LEDs can inactivate microorganisms in drinking water and that the highest inactivation rate constants for E. coli were near 266 nm [N3-F3]. For P. aeruginosa, the peak action spectrum was near 258 nm, and for MS-2, the peak was near 262 nm [N3-F3]. This means that the optimal intensity range is not fixed: it depends on the target microorganism, the application environment, and the desired log reduction. The evidence also notes that polychromatic UV sources can be more effective than single-wavelength lamps because different wavelengths can target proteins and nucleic acids differently [N3-F3]. This suggests that protocol design should match the target organism’s action spectrum and the application’s exposure conditions.

Second, there are trade-offs between intensity, dose, and system throughput. The evidence highlights that UV LEDs can be more efficacious than LP lamps on a fluence basis, but they may require higher electrical efficiency to achieve similar performance on an electrical basis [N3-F3]. It also notes that higher intensity output UV LEDs are more effective on an electrical basis, while fluence-based comparisons depend on the microorganism’s response to applied fluence [N3-F3]. This means that increasing intensity can reduce the time needed to deliver a target dose, but it may also increase energy consumption and reduce throughput if the system cannot handle the power efficiently. The evidence further states that current UV LED efficiencies are low, ranging from 0.01 to 7% EQE between 220 and 285 nm, while some manufacturers have reported higher efficiencies [N3-F3]. This trade-off is important in practice: higher intensity can improve inactivation speed, but it may not be cost-effective if the system requires excessive power or cooling.

Third, operational factors such as suspension state and turbidity modify effectiveness. The evidence on UV disinfection efficiency notes that suspended particles scatter and absorb UV light, lowering microbial inactivation efficiency [N5-R2]. It also states that water quality characteristics can affect UV disinfection, and that the composition of turbidity-causing material was reported as a controlling factor in particle-microorganism association and UV disinfection [N5-R3]. The guidance manual emphasizes that UV light must pass through the whole column of water with sufficient energy to inactivate pathogens [N5-R5]. This means that in suspended or turbid environments, the effective dose is reduced because photons are absorbed or scattered, so higher intensity may be needed to compensate. The evidence also highlights the risks of UV disinfection of unfiltered supplies, underscoring that turbidity and water quality are important operational constraints [N5-R1].

Fourth, intensity and protocol design have implications for disinfection standards and validation. The evidence shows that survival curves and dose-response curves are central to validating disinfection efficacy [N2-F2]. It also states that microbial inactivation curves are used to estimate survivors after UV-C treatment at specific fluence levels [N2-R2][N2-R3]. In practice, the CT (or Ct) concept is challenged on theoretical grounds and its limitations are highlighted [N2-F2]. This implies that standards must account for both intensity and dose, and that validation should go beyond simple fluence measurements. The evidence further indicates that stochastic models can link individual microbial fates to the shape of the survival curve [N2-F2], which supports more rigorous validation methods that capture variability in inactivation outcomes. The practical implication is that protocol design must be validated with realistic operational conditions, including water quality, suspension state, and intensity settings, to ensure compliance with disinfection standards.

Overall, the practical implications are that optimal intensity depends on the microorganism and environment, intensity and dose must be balanced against system throughput and energy use, turbidity and suspension state can strongly reduce effectiveness, and standards and validation should account for intensity-dependent dose-response behavior [N3-F3][N5-R2][N5-R3][N2-F2].

How UV wavelength and lamp type shape inactivation effectiveness and requirements

UV wavelength and lamp type shape inactivation effectiveness and requirements through wavelength-specific DNA absorption, germicidal efficacy, differences in photon delivery and dose uniformity, and effects on repair mechanisms and resistance. The evidence also supports a comparison among 254 nm, 260 nm, and other relevant UV bands.

First, wavelength-specific DNA absorption and germicidal efficacy are central. The evidence states that germicidal efficacy favors wavelengths corresponding closely to the peak absorbance of both nucleic acids and cellular proteins, near 260–280 nm and below 230 nm, respectively [N3-F3]. It also reports that 255–285 nm UV LEDs induce inactivation rate constants for E. coli ranging from 0.15 to 0.81 cm2/mJ, with the highest values closest to the peak of the E. coli action spectrum at 266 nm [N3-F3]. Similarly, P. aeruginosa inactivation by 265–285 nm UV LEDs has inactivation rate constants ranging from 0.51 to 0.74 cm2/mJ, with the peak action spectrum near 258 nm [N3-F3]. MS-2 inactivation by 255–285 nm UV LEDs ranges from 0.029 to 0.076 cm2/mJ, with higher rate constants near 262 nm [N3-F3]. This shows that wavelength strongly influences effectiveness: the closer the wavelength is to the target organism’s peak absorbance, the greater the germicidal efficacy. The evidence also notes that different wavelengths can target different cellular components, such as proteins versus nucleic acids, and that using multiple wavelengths is considered a more effective strategy than a single wavelength [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that wavelength selection should be matched to the target organism and application.

Second, lamp type affects photon delivery and dose uniformity. The evidence highlights that UV LEDs offer tailored wavelengths, low power requirements, flexible design, pulsing, and improved robustness over UV LP lamps without mercury [N3-F3]. It also compares UV LEDs to LP lamps on a fluence basis and on an electrical basis, noting that fluence-based comparisons allow direct comparison of microorganism response without incorporating energy use, while electrical-basis comparisons include the amount of energy required for a given response [N3-F3]. This means that lamp type changes how dose is delivered: LEDs can be designed for specific wavelengths and may allow better control of photon delivery, but LP lamps may have different efficiency and uniformity characteristics. The evidence also states that current UV LED efficiencies are low, with EQE ranging from 0.01 to 7% between 220 and 285 nm, while some manufacturers have achieved higher efficiencies [N3-F3]. This indicates that lamp type affects both the intensity and the energy efficiency of the system, which in turn affects dose delivery and overall effectiveness.

Third, wavelength can affect repair mechanisms and resistance. The evidence shows that some microorganisms require visible light for photoreactivation, while others can repair DNA without light [N4-R4]. This implies that wavelength can influence whether repair mechanisms are activated or not: for example, visible light may be required for photoreactivation, so UV wavelengths that do not overlap with visible light may reduce the opportunity for repair. The review evidence also notes that organisms use photoreactivation, BER, NER, MMR, double-strand break repair, the SOS response, checkpoints, and programmed cell death to counteract UV damage [N1-F1]. This means that wavelength can influence the type and extent of repair, with some wavelengths potentially being more damaging than others because they induce different lesions or different repair responses. The evidence does not provide a detailed comparison of repair efficiency by wavelength, but it does establish that repair mechanisms can reduce the net inactivation effect [N4-R4][N1-F1].

Fourth, the comparison of 254 nm, 260 nm, and other relevant UV bands is supported by the evidence. The evidence states that 254 nm UV-C is highly effective in disinfection and purification applications and is often associated with low-pressure mercury (LP-Hg) lamps [N6-R4][N6-R5]. It also notes that 253.7 nm UV lamps provide powerful germicidal action [N6-R3]. The evidence on LEDs and UV-C inactivation indicates that 255–285 nm UV LEDs can be highly effective, with peak action spectra near 266 nm for E. coli, 258 nm for P. aeruginosa, and 262 nm for MS-2 [N3-F3]. In addition, the evidence states that germicidal efficacy varies with UV-C wavelength and depends on the total exposure or UV dose [N6-R1]. This suggests that 254 nm is often used as a standard germicidal wavelength because of its broad absorption properties and compatibility with LP-Hg lamps [N6-R4][N6-R5], while 260 nm may be more effective for certain organisms because it is closer to their action spectrum [N3-F3]. The evidence also reports that 222 nm UV was less effective than 254 nm for SARS-CoV-2 inactivation in one study [N6-R1], indicating that wavelength choice can greatly affect germicidal requirements.

In conclusion, UV wavelength and lamp type shape inactivation effectiveness and requirements by determining DNA absorption, germicidal efficacy, photon delivery, and repair opportunities. The evidence supports a preference for wavelengths near the target organism’s peak absorbance, such as 260–280 nm for nucleic acids and below 230 nm for proteins [N3-F3], and it shows that lamp type can influence dose delivery and energy efficiency [N3-F3]. The comparison among 254 nm, 260 nm, and other bands indicates that 254 nm is a common and effective standard wavelength, while 260 nm may be more effective for some organisms, and other wavelengths may be preferred depending on the action spectrum and application [N6-R4][N6-R5][N3-F3].

Pulse characteristics can affect how UV photons are delivered and how damage accumulates. The evidence indicates that **pulsed UV light** is delivered several times per second, with pulse durations between **100 ns and 2 ms** [N3-R5]. It also states that **255–285 nm UV LEDs** can inactivate microorganisms in drinking water, and that the wavelength range explored corresponds to the peak absorbance of nucleic acids and cellular proteins [N3-F3]. This suggests that pulse characteristics may influence inactivation depending on the microorganism, wavelength, and duty cycle, but the available evidence is still being explored.

## How does the intensity of irradiation affect these processes?

Irradiation intensity affects UV inactivation through its relationship with **irradiance, dose, and microbial survival**, through **kinetic models** that shape the **dose-response curve**, through **thresholds for inactivation versus sublethal exposure**, and through interactions with **microbial physiology and repair**.

### 1. Relationship between irradiance, dose, and microbial survival

The evidence states that the **dose-response curve** describes the relationship between the number of microbes or their logarithm and the probability of inactivation, with the same term used for both acute illness/death and microbial survival after disinfectant exposure [N2-F2]. It also notes that survival curves show the relationship between UV-C treatment and microbial survivors at specific fluence levels, and that inactivation kinetics can be modeled to estimate survivors after treatment [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This means that higher irradiance can increase the dose delivered more quickly, but the actual survival outcome depends on the total UV dose and how the microorganism responds to that dose. The evidence also notes that the survival curve can resemble a step function when the drop is steep, in which case the **Fermi distribution** becomes suitable, while the **flexible Weibull distribution** and **stochastic models** can describe the underlying vulnerability spectrum [N2-F2]. These findings show that intensity is not the only determinant: dose accumulation and microbial response matter as much as the instantaneous irradiance.

### 2. Kinetic models and how intensity changes the dose-response curve

The evidence highlights that the most notable survival kinetics models in static disinfection are of the **Chick-Watson-Hom** kind, and that their dynamic versions should be viewed with caution [N2-F2]. It also notes that the **flexible Weibull distribution** is a useful mathematical description of the survival curve, with the scale parameter depending on disinfectant intensity, temperature, and other factors [N2-F2]. This implies that intensity can shift the shape of the curve: higher intensity may reduce the number of surviving organisms more rapidly, but the exact relationship depends on the model and the microbial population. The evidence also mentions **stochastic models** that link individual microbial fates to the survival curve’s shape [N2-F2], which suggests that intensity can influence not only the overall survival fraction but also the variability in inactivation outcomes across individuals.

### 3. Thresholds for inactivation versus sublethal exposure

The evidence clearly distinguishes between sublethal and lethal exposure. It states that the same dose-response curve describes both type I (illness/death) and type II (microbial survival) relationships, and that the response is commonly expressed as the percent of inactivated organisms [N2-F2]. The term **LD50** is used as a median lethal dose, where lower LD50 means higher efficacy [N2-F2]. In practice, the evidence reports that UV-C can reduce bacterial populations by several log10 units at high fluence levels, such as **7 log10 reduction at 56 J/mL for Listeria monocytogenes** [N2-R3]. This shows that intensity determines whether the exposure is sublethal or lethal: low-intensity exposure may leave many microbes viable, while higher-intensity exposure can push the system into a steep inactivation phase. The evidence also supports the idea that intensity can shift the response from a gradual decrease in survivors to a more abrupt drop [N2-F2].

### 4. How intensity interacts with microbial physiology and repair

Intensity interacts with microbial physiology and repair mechanisms. The evidence shows that microorganisms have repair mechanisms such as **photoreactivation** and **dark repair** that can reduce the net inactivation effect [N4-R4][N4-R1]. It also notes that organisms use BER, NER, MMR, double-strand break repair, the SOS response, checkpoints, and programmed cell death to counteract UV damage [N1-F1]. This means that higher intensity can overwhelm repair capacity, but if repair mechanisms are effective, they can offset some of the damage. The evidence further indicates that microbial tolerance to UV-B varies across species and taxonomic groups, and that increased UV exposure can be predicted to continue throughout much of this century because of ozone depletion [N1-F1]. This physiological variability implies that intensity does not act uniformly: some microbes may survive higher doses because they repair faster or have more resistance, while others may be killed more readily.

## Integrated synthesis: mechanisms and intensity dependence together

The most important takeaway is that UV inactivation is a **composite process** involving both **direct DNA damage** and **indirect ROS-mediated damage**, with repair and resistance mechanisms acting as counterforces. At the same time, **irradiation intensity** is central to how quickly and how effectively these processes unfold. Higher intensity can deliver more dose more rapidly, but it does not guarantee higher efficacy because the **dose-response relationship is nonlinear** and depends on **microbial physiology, repair capacity, and environmental conditions**.

Pulsed UV adds another layer of complexity. This implies that pulse design can be useful, but it should be tailored to the organism, wavelength, and system requirements.

Overall, pulsed UV radiation inactivates microorganisms mainly through **direct DNA damage**, **ROS-mediated indirect damage**, and **repair mechanisms**, while **intensity** affects the process by changing the **dose**, the **shape of the dose-response curve**, the **threshold for inactivation**, and the **interaction with microbial physiology and repair** [N1-F1][N1-R3][N4-R4][N2-F2]. This means that the optimal intensity range is not fixed: it depends on the target microorganism, the application environment, and the desired log reduction. The evidence also notes that polychromatic UV sources can be more effective than single-wavelength lamps because different wavelengths can target proteins and nucleic acids differently [N3-F3]. This suggests that protocol design should match the target organism’s action spectrum and the application’s exposure conditions.

Second, there are trade-offs between intensity, dose, and system throughput. The evidence highlights that UV LEDs can be more efficacious than LP lamps on a fluence basis, but they may require higher electrical efficiency to achieve similar performance on an electrical basis [N3-F3]. It also notes that higher intensity output UV LEDs are more effective on an electrical basis, while fluence-based comparisons depend on the microorganism’s response to applied fluence [N3-F3]. This means that increasing intensity can reduce the time needed to deliver a target dose, but it may also increase energy consumption and reduce throughput if the system cannot handle the power efficiently. The evidence further states that current UV LED efficiencies are low, ranging from 0.01 to 7% EQE between 220 and 285 nm, while some manufacturers have reported higher efficiencies [N3-F3]. This trade-off is important in practice: higher intensity can improve inactivation speed, but it may not be cost-effective if the system requires excessive power or cooling.

The evidence on UV disinfection efficiency notes that suspended particles scatter and absorb UV light, lowering microbial inactivation efficiency [N5-R2]. It also states that water quality characteristics can affect UV disinfection, and that the composition of turbidity-causing material was reported as a controlling factor in particle-microorganism association and UV disinfection [N5-R3]. This means that in suspended or turbid environments, the effective dose is reduced because photons are absorbed or scattered, so higher intensity may be needed to compensate. ## What are the main mechanisms through which pulsed UV radiation inactivates microorganisms?

Pulsed UV radiation inactivates microorganisms primarily through **direct DNA damage**, **generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and indirect damage pathways**, and through the **repair and resistance mechanisms** that microorganisms use to counteract these effects. Pulse characteristics such as **duty cycle and pulse duration** also influence how UV photons are delivered and how damage accumulates over time.

### 1. Direct DNA damage induced by UV photons

The central molecular mechanism is damage to DNA. The evidence states that UV-induced DNA damage occurs most notably through the induction of **cyclobutane-pyrimidine dimers (CPDs), 6-4 photoproducts (6-4PPs), and their Dewar valence isomers**, as well as **DNA strand breaks** [N1-F1]. This damage disrupts the DNA helix and can block replication and transcription, which is why DNA is described as one of the prime targets of UV radiation [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that organisms have developed several highly conserved repair mechanisms to counteract these lesions, including **photoreactivation, base excision repair (BER), nucleotide excision repair (NER), mismatch repair (MMR), double-strand break repair, the SOS response, cell-cycle checkpoints, and programmed cell death** [N1-F1].

### 2. Reactive oxygen species and indirect damage pathways

UV radiation can also generate **reactive oxygen species (ROS)** and cause indirect damage. The evidence explicitly states that **oxidative damage** can be caused by direct interaction of ionizing radiations with DNA molecules, as well as mediated by **UV radiation-induced free radicals or reactive oxygen species** [N1-F1]. It also reports that irradiation with **254-nm UVC** has been associated with ROS generation involved in the germicidal mechanism [N1-R3]. This means that even when UV photons do not directly hit DNA, they can still damage microorganisms by creating ROS that oxidize DNA or other cellular components. However, the evidence provided does not give a detailed mechanism of ROS-mediated inactivation beyond this general statement, so this should be treated as established but not fully elaborated in the available material.

### 3. Microbial repair and resistance mechanisms that mitigate inactivation

Microbial repair and resistance mechanisms can significantly reduce the effectiveness of UV inactivation. The evidence identifies **photoreactivation** and **dark repair** as mechanisms that reverse UV-induced DNA damage [N4-R4][N4-R1]. It also notes that some microorganisms require visible light for **photoreactivation**, while others can repair DNA without light [N4-R4]. The review evidence further lists several repair pathways, including BER, NER, MMR, double-strand break repair, the SOS response, checkpoints, and programmed cell death [N1-F1]. These mechanisms help microorganisms survive or recover after UV exposure, thereby reducing the net inactivation effect.

### 4. How pulse characteristics influence photon delivery and damage accumulation

Pulse characteristics can affect how UV photons are delivered and how damage accumulates. The evidence indicates that **pulsed UV light** is delivered several times per second, with pulse durations between **100 ns and 2 ms** [N3-R5]. It also states that **255–285 nm UV LEDs** can inactivate microorganisms in drinking water, and that the wavelength range explored corresponds to the peak absorbance of nucleic acids and cellular proteins [N3-F3]. However, the evidence is mixed: one study found **no difference in disinfection** between pulsed and continuous UV LEDs, while another reported that **pulsed UV-C radiation at 260 nm** produced significantly greater log reductions than continuous UV-C for **E. coli** and **B. subtilis** [N3-R1][N3-R2]. This suggests that pulse characteristics may influence inactivation depending on the microorganism, wavelength, and duty cycle, but the available evidence is still being explored.

## How does the intensity of irradiation affect these processes?

Irradiation intensity affects UV inactivation through its relationship with **irradiance, dose, and microbial survival**, through **kinetic models** that shape the **dose-response curve**, through **thresholds for inactivation versus sublethal exposure**, and through interactions with **microbial physiology and repair**.

### 1. Relationship between irradiance, dose, and microbial survival

The evidence states that the **dose-response curve** describes the relationship between the number of microbes or their logarithm and the probability of inactivation, with the same term used for both acute illness/death and microbial survival after disinfectant exposure [N2-F2]. It also notes that survival curves show the relationship between UV-C treatment and microbial survivors at specific fluence levels, and that inactivation kinetics can be modeled to estimate survivors after treatment [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This means that higher irradiance can increase the dose delivered more quickly, but the actual survival outcome depends on the total UV dose and how the microorganism responds to that dose. The evidence also notes that the survival curve can resemble a step function when the drop is steep, in which case the **Fermi distribution** becomes suitable, while the **flexible Weibull distribution** and **stochastic models** can describe the underlying vulnerability spectrum [N2-F2]. These findings show that intensity is not the only determinant: dose accumulation and microbial response matter as much as the instantaneous irradiance.

### 2. Kinetic models and how intensity changes the dose-response curve

The evidence highlights that the most notable survival kinetics models in static disinfection are of the **Chick-Watson-Hom** kind, and that their dynamic versions should be viewed with caution [N2-F2]. It also notes that the **flexible Weibull distribution** is a useful mathematical description of the survival curve, with the scale parameter depending on disinfectant intensity, temperature, and other factors [N2-F2]. This implies that intensity can shift the shape of the curve: higher intensity may reduce the number of surviving organisms more rapidly, but the exact relationship depends on the model and the microbial population. The evidence also mentions **stochastic models** that link individual microbial fates to the survival curve’s shape [N2-F2], which suggests that intensity can influence not only the overall survival fraction but also the variability in inactivation outcomes across individuals.

### 3. Thresholds for inactivation versus sublethal exposure

The evidence clearly distinguishes between sublethal and lethal exposure. It states that the same dose-response curve describes both type I (illness/death) and type II (microbial survival) relationships, and that the response is commonly expressed as the percent of inactivated organisms [N2-F2]. The term **LD50** is used as a median lethal dose, where lower LD50 means higher efficacy [N2-F2]. In practice, the evidence reports that UV-C can reduce bacterial populations by several log10 units at high fluence levels, such as **7 log10 reduction at 56 J/mL for Listeria monocytogenes** [N2-R3]. This shows that intensity determines whether the exposure is sublethal or lethal: low-intensity exposure may leave many microbes viable, while higher-intensity exposure can push the system into a steep inactivation phase. The evidence also supports the idea that intensity can shift the response from a gradual decrease in survivors to a more abrupt drop [N2-F2].

### 4. How intensity interacts with microbial physiology and repair

Intensity interacts with microbial physiology and repair mechanisms. The evidence shows that microorganisms have repair mechanisms such as **photoreactivation** and **dark repair** that can reduce the net inactivation effect [N4-R4][N4-R1]. It also notes that organisms use BER, NER, MMR, double-strand break repair, the SOS response, checkpoints, and programmed cell death to counteract UV damage [N1-F1]. This means that higher intensity can overwhelm repair capacity, but if repair mechanisms are effective, they can offset some of the damage. The evidence further indicates that microbial tolerance to UV-B varies across species and taxonomic groups, and that increased UV exposure can be predicted to continue throughout much of this century because of ozone depletion [N1-F1]. This physiological variability implies that intensity does not act uniformly: some microbes may survive higher doses because they repair faster or have more resistance, while others may be killed more readily.

## Integrated synthesis: mechanisms and intensity dependence together

The most important takeaway is that UV inactivation is a **composite process** involving both **direct DNA damage** and **indirect ROS-mediated damage**, with repair and resistance mechanisms acting as counterforces. At the same time, **irradiation intensity** is central to how quickly and how effectively these processes unfold. Higher intensity can deliver more dose more rapidly, but it does not guarantee higher efficacy because the **dose-response relationship is nonlinear** and depends on **microbial physiology, repair capacity, and environmental conditions**.

Pulsed UV adds another layer of complexity. The evidence suggests that pulse characteristics can influence damage accumulation, but the results are mixed: some studies show no difference between pulsed and continuous UV LEDs, while others report greater log reductions with pulsed UV-C at specific wavelengths [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. This implies that pulse design can be useful, but it should be tailored to the organism, wavelength, and system requirements.

The practical implications are also clear. Optimal intensity ranges vary with **microorganism**, **environment**, and **application** because different organisms have different **action spectra** and different repair capacities [N3-F3][N1-F1]. Higher intensity can improve inactivation speed, but it may also increase energy use and reduce throughput if the system is inefficient [N3-F3]. Operational factors such as **suspension state** and **turbidity** can strongly reduce effectiveness because suspended particles scatter and absorb UV light, lowering microbial inactivation efficiency [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Finally, disinfection standards and validation must account for **intensity-dependent dose-response behavior**, because the CT (or Ct) concept is challenged on theoretical grounds and its limitations are highlighted [N2-F2].

## Conclusion

Overall, pulsed UV radiation inactivates microorganisms mainly through **direct DNA damage**, **ROS-mediated indirect damage**, and **repair mechanisms**, while **intensity** affects the process by changing the **dose**, the **shape of the dose-response curve**, the **threshold for inactivation**, and the **interaction with microbial physiology and repair** [N1-F1][N1-R3][N4-R4][N2-F2]. The evidence supports a nuanced picture in which effectiveness depends not only on the UV source itself but also on the organism’s repair capacity, the environment, and the design of the irradiation protocol [N3-F3][N5-R2][N2-F2].

The central molecular mechanism is damage to DNA. This damage disrupts the DNA helix and can block replication and transcription, which is why DNA is described as one of the prime targets of UV radiation [N1-F1]. ### 2. Reactive oxygen species and indirect damage pathways

UV radiation can also generate **reactive oxygen species (ROS)** and cause indirect damage. The evidence explicitly states that **oxidative damage** can be caused by direct interaction of ionizing radiations with DNA molecules, as well as mediated by **UV radiation-induced free radicals or reactive oxygen species** [N1-F1]. It also reports that irradiation with **254-nm UVC** has been associated with ROS generation involved in the germicidal mechanism [N1-R3]. This means that even when UV photons do not directly hit DNA, they can still damage microorganisms by creating ROS that oxidize DNA or other cellular components. However, the evidence provided does not give a detailed mechanism of ROS-mediated inactivation beyond this general statement, so this should be treated as established but not fully elaborated in the available material.

Microbial repair and resistance mechanisms can significantly reduce the effectiveness of UV inactivation. The evidence identifies **photoreactivation** and **dark repair** as mechanisms that reverse UV-induced DNA damage [N4-R4][N4-R1]. These mechanisms help microorganisms survive or recover after UV exposure, thereby reducing the net inactivation effect.

### 4. How pulse characteristics influence photon delivery and damage accumulation

Pulse characteristics can affect how UV photons are delivered and how damage accumulates. The evidence indicates that **pulsed UV light** is delivered several times per second, with pulse durations between **100 ns and 2 ms** [N3-R5]. It also states that **255–285 nm UV LEDs** can inactivate microorganisms in drinking water, and that the wavelength range explored corresponds to the peak absorbance of nucleic acids and cellular proteins [N3-F3]. The evidence highlights that the most notable survival kinetics models in static disinfection are of the **Chick-Watson-Hom** kind, and that their dynamic versions should be viewed with caution [N2-F2]. This implies that pulse design can be useful, but it should be tailored to the organism, wavelength, and system requirements.

The practical implications are also clear. Higher intensity can improve inactivation speed, but it may also increase energy use and reduce throughput if the system is inefficient [N3-F3]. Overall, pulsed UV radiation inactivates microorganisms mainly through **direct DNA damage**, **ROS-mediated indirect damage**, and **repair mechanisms**, while **intensity** affects the process by changing the **dose**, the **shape of the dose-response curve**, the **threshold for inactivation**, and the **interaction with microbial physiology and repair** [N1-F1][N1-R3][N4-R4][N2-F2].
